course: How to Start a Business in Africa

lessons.title: Setting Up Efficient Operations
lessons.body:
In Africa, efficient operations start with mapping your core process on paper. For a small bakery in Ghana, that means listing every step from buying flour to selling bread. Identify bottlenecks: maybe your oven can only bake 50 loaves per hour, but you sell 80. That gap costs you sales. Simple tools like a stopwatch and a notebook help. Time each step for a week. You'll likely find that 20% of steps cause 80% of delays.

Next, design your workspace for flow. In many African cities, space is tight and expensive. Use vertical storage: shelves up to the ceiling for ingredients. Keep frequently used items within arm's reach. For a tailoring business in Kenya, arrange sewing machines in a U-shape so fabric moves clockwise without crossing paths. This can cut production time by 15-20%.

Standardize repetitive tasks. Write simple one-page checklists for opening and closing. For a food vendor, a morning checklist might include: clean grill, chop onions, check gas level. This reduces mistakes and training time. Use cheap laminated cards or a WhatsApp group to share daily tasks.

Finally, measure daily output and waste. If you produce 100 units but 10 are defective, your efficiency is 90%. Track this number on a wall chart. Aim to improve by 5% each month. In low-infrastructure settings, even small gains matter. Remember, efficiency isn't about working harder; it's about removing wasted motion, time, and materials.

lessons.title: Sourcing Raw Materials Locally
lessons.body:
Sourcing locally cuts costs and lead times. In Nigeria, a soap maker can buy palm oil from nearby farmers instead of importing from Malaysia. Local sourcing reduces transport costs by 30-50% and supports the community. Start by visiting local markets or using apps like FarmCrowdy or Thrive Agric to connect with farmers.

Negotiate directly with producers. For a maize miller in Tanzania, buying directly from smallholder farmers at harvest time (June-August) can be 20% cheaper than buying from middlemen. Offer to pay cash on delivery. Build relationships: visit farms, agree on quality standards, and sign simple contracts. A handshake plus a written note works in many rural areas.

Consider forming a buying group with other businesses. In Uganda, five restaurants can pool orders for fresh vegetables, getting bulk discounts and sharing delivery costs. Use a WhatsApp group to coordinate weekly orders. This also gives you bargaining power.

Quality control is key. Inspect every batch. For a textile business in Ethiopia, check cotton for moisture and debris. Reject poor quality immediately. Set clear specs: e.g., 'moisture below 10%, no stones.' Pay fairly and on time to keep suppliers loyal. Local sourcing isn't just cheaper; it makes your supply chain resilient to import delays and currency fluctuations.

lessons.title: Managing Logistics and Transportation
lessons.body:
In Africa, moving goods is often the biggest cost. A 2020 study found that logistics can be 40-60% of product cost in landlocked countries. To manage this, start by mapping your routes. For a distributor in Rwanda, moving from Kigali to Kampala might take 12 hours by road, but border delays can add 6 hours. Use Google Maps to plan, but always add buffer time.

Choose the right transport mode. For small, high-value items like phone accessories, use motorbike taxis (boda boda) for same-day delivery within cities. For bulk goods like cement, hire a 7-ton truck. Negotiate rates: in Kenya, a 7-ton truck from Nairobi to Mombasa costs about KES 40,000. Get three quotes. Consider backhauling: if a truck returns empty, you can negotiate a 30% discount.

Consolidate shipments. Instead of sending three small vans, send one larger truck. For a cosmetics distributor in Ghana, consolidating orders from Accra to Kumasi twice a week instead of daily cut transport costs by 25%. Use a simple spreadsheet to track shipments: date, driver, vehicle number, expected arrival, actual arrival.

Finally, use technology. Apps like Sendy (Kenya) or Kobo360 (Nigeria) connect you to vetted transporters. They handle tracking and insurance. For cross-border, use clearing agents who know customs. Always insure goods; a single accident can wipe out your profit. Keep a log of delays and costs to improve over time.

lessons.title: Overcoming Infrastructure Hurdles
lessons.body:
Infrastructure in Africa is improving but still unreliable. Power cuts, poor roads, and water shortages are common. To survive, you need backups. For power, invest in a small generator or solar panel. A 1.5 kVA generator costs about $200 and can run lights, a fridge, and a laptop. Solar panels with battery storage cost $500-$1000 but save fuel in the long run. In Nigeria, many businesses use inverters to keep going during outages.

For water, drill a borehole if you can afford it (cost: $3,000-$8,000). Otherwise, store water in tanks. A 1,000-liter tank costs $100. For a restaurant in Tanzania, having two days' water supply prevents closure during shortages.

Roads are often bad, especially in rainy season. Plan deliveries around weather. In Malawi, a farmer might harvest maize in April but wait until May to transport because roads are muddy. Use smaller vehicles that can navigate rough roads. Or, use motorbikes for last-mile delivery. In Ethiopia, a coffee cooperative uses donkeys to bring beans from remote farms to a collection point.

Internet connectivity can be spotty. Use mobile money (M-Pesa, MTN MoMo) for payments. Keep cash as backup. For communication, use SMS instead of WhatsApp when data is down. Train staff to handle these challenges calmly. Document what works and build redundancy into every critical process.

lessons.title: Quality Control and Standards
lessons.body:
Quality is your reputation. In Africa, where counterfeit goods are common, consistent quality sets you apart. Start by defining standards for your product. For a honey producer in Zambia, that means: moisture content below 20%, no added sugar, clean jars. Write these down and share with your team.

Inspect raw materials and finished goods. Use simple tests. For a maize flour mill, check for aflatoxin using a $50 test kit from a local lab. For a soap maker, test pH with litmus paper. Reject any batch that fails. Keep records: date, batch number, result. This helps trace problems.

Train your workers on quality. A 2-hour session on handwashing and hygiene can reduce contamination. For a garment factory in Lesotho, teach seamstresses to check stitches per inch. Use a checklist for each item before packing.

Get certified if possible. For food products, HACCP or ISO 22000 certification opens export markets. In Kenya, KEBS certification is required for many products. The process takes time but builds trust. Even without certification, display your standards on packaging: '100% natural' or 'no preservatives'.

Finally, listen to customers. A simple feedback form or WhatsApp number can reveal defects. If three customers complain about the same issue, fix it immediately. Quality control is not a one-time event; it's a daily habit.

lessons.title: Inventory Management and Technology Adoption
lessons.body:
Inventory ties up cash. In Africa, where credit is expensive, overstocking can kill your business. Start by categorizing items: A (high value, low volume), B (medium), C (low value, high volume). For a pharmacy in Ghana, A items are antibiotics, C items are bandages. Count A items daily, B weekly, C monthly.

Use the 80/20 rule: 20% of items generate 80% of sales. Focus on those. Set reorder points: when stock hits a certain level, order more. For a shop selling phone chargers, if you sell 10 per day and delivery takes 3 days, reorder when you have 30 left. Use a simple notebook or Excel sheet. For better control, use free apps like Zoho Inventory or Sortly. They work offline and sync when you have data.

Adopt technology step by step. Start with mobile money to track payments. Then use a barcode scanner ($30) and a laptop for inventory. In Kenya, small shops use M-Pesa to pay suppliers and record sales via SMS. For larger operations, consider a POS system like Vend or Kopo Kopo. These cost $20-$50 per month but reduce theft and stockouts.

Train your staff on the system. A one-day workshop is enough. Keep a backup of all data on a USB drive or cloud. Review inventory reports weekly. If you have slow-moving stock, discount it to free up cash. Remember, technology is a tool, not a solution. The goal is to know what you have, where it is, and when to reorder.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Operations & Supply Chain Management in African Agribusiness

This practical reference consolidates the operational tools, benchmarks, and decision rules you need to run a small or growing agribusiness in Africa. It is written for founders, operations managers, and cooperative leaders who must move physical goods â seed, produce, feed, processed food â through real infrastructure constraints. Each section gives you a usable instrument: a cost model, a sourcing rule, a logistics decision, a quality protocol, or an inventory method.

Treat this as a working document. Print it, annotate it, and attach your own numbers. The benchmarks below are drawn from official African and international sources so you can defend your assumptions to lenders and investors.

1. Setting Up Efficient Operations

Efficiency in African agribusiness is rarely about automation. It is about eliminating waiting time, double-handling, and rework. Start with a simple process map for your top three products. Identify every point where a person touches, moves, or waits for the product. Each is a cost and a loss risk.

Design for the constraint you actually have: unreliable grid power, seasonal labour, or a single unreliable road. A poultry processor in Ghana, for example, may run two shifts on generator power only during peak demand periods rather than paying for 24-hour diesel. A grain miller in Tanzania may schedule milling around the rainy season when transport costs spike.

Key operational metrics to track weekly: units processed per labour hour, downtime hours, rework percentage, and cost per unit output. If you cannot measure it, you cannot improve it.

2. Sourcing Raw Materials Locally

Local sourcing reduces forex exposure, transport cost, and lead time â but it requires active supplier development. Do not assume smallholder supply is automatically cheaper or more reliable. Build a supplier scorecard covering: volume consistency, quality grade, delivery punctuality, price stability, and payment terms.

Practical rules: contract with at least three suppliers per critical input; pay within agreed terms to build loyalty; provide inputs or training on credit only where you can enforce collection via off-take. For grains and pulses, test moisture content and aflatoxin before accepting delivery.

Table 1. Typical input sourcing cost structure for a small agri-processor in East Africa (illustrative, % of landed input cost)
Cost element Local sourcing Imported sourcing Notes
Base material price55â70%45â60%Imported base often lower per tonne
Inland transport8â15%12â22%Port-to-factory leg is costly
Clearing & duties0â3%10â20%Tariffs, VAT, agent fees
Forex & financing1â3%4â10%LC charges, hedging, delay cost
Quality rejection / loss3â8%2â5%Local supply more variable
Lead time (days)3â1430â90Working capital impact

Source: Author's synthesis of cost structures reported in World Bank, Africa's Pulse (2023) and FAO agribusiness value-chain studies. Figures are indicative and vary by country, commodity, and scale.

3. Managing Logistics and Transportation

Transport is often the single largest controllable cost after raw materials. In many African markets, road freight rates are 2â4 times higher per tonne-kilometre than in developed economies, driven by poor road quality, border delays, and empty backhauls.

Three levers: consolidate loads, negotiate backhaul rates, and plan routes around known bottlenecks (weighbridges, border posts, market days). For perishables, pre-cool and use insulated or refrigerated transport only where the price premium justifies it. Otherwise, move at night and minimise time at ambient temperature.

Table 2. Indicative road freight cost and transit time benchmarks, selected African corridors (2023)
Corridor Approx. distance (km) Cost (US$/tonne-km) Typical transit time Main bottleneck
MombasaâNairobiâKampala1,2000.06â0.104â8 daysBorder clearance, weighbridges
DurbanâJohannesburgâHarare1,6000.05â0.095â10 daysBorder delays, road condition
LagosâKano1,0000.08â0.143â6 daysRoad quality, checkpoints

Source: World Bank, Africa's Pulse and the Sub-Saharan Africa Transport Policy Program (SSATP) corridor performance reports, 2022â2023. Rates are indicative and exclude demurrage, informal payments, and spoilage.

4. Overcoming Infrastructure Hurdles

Assume grid power will fail, water will be intermittent, and roads will be impassable for part of the year. Build redundancy into the smallest viable unit: a backup generator sized for critical loads only, a rainwater or borehole backup, and a secondary route or supplier.

Where cold chain is unreliable, use evaporative cooling, solar-powered cold rooms, or hermetic storage bags. Where mobile coverage is weak, use offline-first inventory apps that sync when connectivity returns.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Aflatoxin and Food Safety

Do not accept or sell maize, groundnuts, or other susceptible crops with visible mould or a musty smell. Aflatoxin contamination is invisible at low levels, is not destroyed by normal cooking, and causes liver damage and stunting in children. Test every incoming lot with a rapid test kit or accredited lab before processing or sale. Store at <13% moisture. Reject any lot above the national regulatory limit (commonly 10 ppb total aflatoxin for food in many African jurisdictions; check your national standard). Never blend contaminated grain with clean grain to "dilute" it â this is illegal and dangerous.

5. Quality Control and Standards

Quality is a market-access issue, not just a compliance cost. Buyers, processors, and exporters increasingly require documented food safety systems. For most small and medium agribusinesses, the practical pathway is:

  • Good Hygiene Practice (GHP) and Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) â basic cleanliness, pest control, personnel hygiene, water quality.
  • HACCP â hazard analysis and critical control points for your specific process.
  • ISO 22000 or FSSC 22000 â only when a buyer demands certification and will pay for it.
  • National standards â e.g., KEBS (Kenya), NAFDAC (Nigeria), Ghana Standards Authority, SABS (South Africa).

Document everything: supplier batch numbers, incoming inspection results, process temperatures, cleaning logs, and final product tests. If a buyer recalls your product, traceability is your only defence.

6. Inventory Management and Technology Adoption

Inventory is cash sitting on a shelf, and in agribusiness it can rot. Use the simplest system that gives you accurate stock counts and reorder triggers. For many small businesses, a spreadsheet with daily counts and a two-bin system (one active bin, one reserve) is enough. Move to a cloud or offline-capable inventory app when you have more than 50 SKUs or multiple locations.

Set reorder points based on lead time and demand variability, not on gut feel. For perishables, use FIFO (first-in, first-out) strictly and track shelf life by batch. For non-perishables, calculate economic order quantity only where storage cost is real; otherwise prioritise supplier reliability and cash flow.

Technology that actually pays back in African agribusiness: mobile money for supplier and customer payments, SMS/USSD for farmer communication, GPS for fleet tracking, and simple barcode or QR scanning for batch traceability. Avoid complex ERP systems until your processes are stable.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Map your process. Identify every touch, move, and wait point for your top three products. Eliminate one waste per month.
  2. Qualify at least three suppliers per critical input. Score them monthly on quality, delivery, and price.
  3. Test every incoming lot for moisture and aflatoxin where relevant. Reject contaminated material. Document results.
  4. Consolidate loads and negotiate backhauls. Track cost per tonne-km and transit time by route.
  5. Build redundancy for power, water, and transport. Size backup for critical loads only.
  6. Implement GHP and a HACCP plan before seeking certification. Train staff and keep logs.
  7. Use FIFO and batch tracking for all perishables. Set reorder points using lead time and demand variability.
  8. Adopt only technology that pays back within 12 months. Start with mobile money, SMS, and simple inventory apps.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â The State of Food and Agriculture 2019: Moving forward on food loss and waste reduction
  • World Bank â Africa's Pulse (latest edition)
  • SSATP â Sub-Saharan Africa Transport Policy Program: Corridor Performance Reports
  • WHO/FAO â Codex Alimentarius: General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969)
  • IFC â Agribusiness and Food Safety Standards: Practical Guides for SMEs

quiz.q: What is the first step to setting up efficient operations?
options: B) Map your core process on paper
quiz.explanation: Mapping the process helps identify bottlenecks and wasted steps before making changes.

quiz.q: In a tailoring business, arranging sewing machines in a U-shape can cut production time by how much?
quiz.explanation: U-shaped layout reduces crossing paths and improves flow, saving 15-20% of time.

quiz.q: Why is local sourcing often cheaper?
quiz.explanation: Local sourcing cuts transport costs by 30-50% and avoids import delays.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of forming a buying group?
quiz.explanation: Pooling orders gives bargaining power and reduces per-unit costs.

quiz.q: In Africa, logistics can account for what percentage of product cost?
quiz.explanation: Studies show logistics can be 40-60% of product cost, especially in landlocked countries.

quiz.q: What is backhauling?
options: B) Negotiating a discount on a return trip
quiz.explanation: Backhauling means using a truck's return trip to carry goods at a discount.

quiz.q: Which app connects businesses to vetted transporters in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Sendy is a logistics platform that connects businesses with transporters.

quiz.q: What is a common infrastructure hurdle in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Power cuts are frequent and require backups like generators or solar.

quiz.q: How can a business overcome water shortages?
quiz.explanation: Drilling a borehole or storing water in tanks ensures continuous supply.

quiz.q: What is a simple quality test for honey?
quiz.explanation: Moisture content below 20% prevents fermentation and ensures quality.

quiz.q: Why is quality control important for African businesses?
quiz.explanation: Consistent quality builds trust and sets you apart from counterfeit goods.

quiz.q: What does HACCP certification cover?
quiz.explanation: HACCP is a food safety management system that opens export markets.

quiz.q: What is the 80/20 rule in inventory?
options: A) 80% of items give 20% of sales
B) 20% of items give 80% of sales
quiz.explanation: Focus on the 20% of items that generate 80% of sales.

quiz.q: What is a reorder point?
options: A) When to order more stock
quiz.explanation: Reorder point is the stock level that triggers a new order.

quiz.q: Which free app can help with inventory management?
quiz.explanation: Zoho Inventory is a free tool for tracking stock, works offline.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using mobile money for inventory?
options: A) It tracks payments and sales
quiz.explanation: Mobile money like M-Pesa provides a record of transactions and reduces cash handling.

quiz.q: What should you do with slow-moving stock?
options: B) Discount it to free cash
quiz.explanation: Discounting slow movers frees up cash for better-selling items.

quiz.q: How often should you count A items in inventory?
quiz.explanation: A items are high value, so daily counts prevent theft and stockouts.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to track shipments?
quiz.explanation: Any of these can work, but a spreadsheet is easy to update and share.

quiz.q: Why is consolidating shipments beneficial?
quiz.explanation: Consolidating orders into one larger shipment lowers per-unit transport cost.

quiz.q: What is a common challenge with roads in rainy season?
quiz.explanation: Muddy roads can block transport, so plan around weather.

quiz.q: What is a low-cost backup for power?
quiz.explanation: Generators, solar panels, and inverters all provide backup power.

quiz.q: What is a simple quality check for soap?
options: A) pH test with litmus paper
quiz.explanation: pH testing ensures soap is safe for skin.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records of quality tests?
quiz.explanation: Records help identify and fix quality issues quickly.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of training workers on quality?
quiz.explanation: Trained workers make fewer mistakes, improving overall quality.

quiz.q: What does KEBS stand for?
quiz.explanation: KEBS is the Kenya Bureau of Standards, which certifies products.

quiz.q: What is a good way to get customer feedback?
quiz.explanation: A dedicated WhatsApp number makes it easy for customers to report issues.

quiz.q: What is the goal of inventory management?
options: A) To have as much stock as possible
B) To know what you have and when to reorder
D) To only stock A items
quiz.explanation: Inventory management ensures you have the right stock at the right time.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using a barcode scanner?
quiz.explanation: Barcode scanners speed up stocktaking and reduce human error.

quiz.q: What should you do with inventory data?
quiz.explanation: Backing up data prevents loss and ensures continuity.
